title: Two knowledges
hookLine: a great householder asks for the one thing that, once known, makes everything known, and hears that even the Vedas count as the lower knowledge
carry: the vedas are lower; knowing the imperishable is higher
tomorrow: how does one thing become everything?
last: SATYA: I DON'T KNOW IS BETTER THAN A LIE.

lines: ONE THING THAT MAKES SENSE OF ALL?
cards: A library with every book ever written. A whole lifetime in it might get you through one shelf. Then someone walks in and asks the librarian: is there one thing I could know, and then everything else would make sense?
That's how the Mundaka opens. Shaunaka, a great householder, comes properly, as a student should, to the sage Angiras, and asks: Sir, what is it that, when it is known, all of this becomes known?
And Angiras starts by dividing every kind of knowing in two.

teach.h: WHAT, ONCE KNOWN, MAKES ALL KNOWN?
teach.b: The Mundaka belongs to the Atharva Veda, and it opens with its own family tree. Brahma, first of the gods, taught this knowledge to his eldest son, Atharvan, and it passed teacher to student down to Angiras.
Then Shaunaka asks his question, and Angiras says: two knowledges are to be known, so say those who know Brahman.
The higher, and the lower. Then the surprise.

teach.h: EVEN THE FOUR VEDAS ARE THE LOWER.
teach.b: The lower knowledge is the Rig Veda, the Yajur Veda, the Sama Veda, the Atharva Veda, and with them phonetics, ritual, grammar, the study of words, meter and astronomy, the six sciences that serve the Vedas.
And the higher? That by which the imperishable is grasped. Akshara, the one that doesn't wear away.
Notice where this is said. Not by a critic outside the tradition. Inside the Atharva Veda itself, the Veda calls its own recitation the lower knowledge.
Shankara reads the lower as knowledge of words and rites, and the higher as the direct knowing the words point to. No one in the story throws the Vedas away. Shaunaka learned them.
Angiras learned them. They're the ladder you climb, and the Upanishad is part of the Veda too. The point is what kind of knowing it is.
You can know everything about a mango, its region, its chemistry, its price, and never have tasted one. The lower knowledge is everything about. The higher is the taste.
That's the teaching: para vidya, the higher knowing, is knowing Brahman directly, and in this tradition all the study is there to point you to it.

how: In traditional Vedic schools students still memorize the Vedas and study the six auxiliary sciences, the vedangas, and Vedanta teachers use the Mundaka's two knowledges to explain why study is a ladder rather than the goal.

the six sciences that serve the Vedas

it belongs to the Atharva Veda. the Veda calls its own recitation the lower knowledge.
the lower knowledge includes grammar, meter and astronomy
the six sciences that serve the Vedas are listed with them.

games.q: you're Angiras. a great householder asks what single thing, once known, makes everything known. how do you begin?
o: say there are two knowledges, higher and lower.
games.why: two knowledges are to be known. the lower is the Vedas and their sciences; the higher is that by which the imperishable is grasped.

practice: Think of something you know a lot about, a song, a recipe, a person, and run through the facts you know. Then set the facts aside and remember what it's actually like: the taste, the sound, the feel of being with them.
If you'd like, turn toward this moment the same way: not facts about it, just what it's like to be here.

wordCard.voice: Akshara, the imperishable, what doesn't wear away. In the Mundaka, the lower knowledge is the Vedas and their sciences; the higher is that by which it is grasped.

orig.note: Sanskrit akṣara, the imperishable: a, not, + kṣara, wasting away. the object of the higher knowledge.

carryVoice: Your line: the Vedas are lower; knowing the imperishable is higher. Tomorrow, a spider shows how one thing becomes everything. Day four hundred eleven, done.
